bibliography_fields.included: Selected complete Ahirwati grammatical description pp. 49--51, Gurgaon specimen 37 pp. 233--236 and mixed Jhajjar/Rohtak specimen 38 pp. 237--239, with the explicit Bagri comparison spans on pp. 149 and 151. No Ahirwati column is printed in the volume's standard comparative tables.
bibliography_fields.note: The original title retains THE before Rajasthani and Gujarati; the 1927 minor addenda p. 41 directs its omission. The source calls Ahirwati a Mewati variety and explicitly qualifies specimen 38 as mixed with Bangaru. The quoted Bagri comparisons distinguish Sirsa, Hissar and Bikaner. The author attributes the second-person plural present sai with nasalization to borrowing from Bagri; that attributed claim does not identify a specific printed donor occurrence.

repeated_notes.notes: Grierson gives apᵃṇū/apᵃṇō as ‘own’ and apᵃṇā as the masculine oblique.
Grierson describes nē̃ as both the dative and agent-case suffix; this occurrence is glossed with “by”.
The printed final component sai matches a copula in Grierson’s p. 51 paradigm; this comparison does not classify the entire compound.
Source says these occur in Sirsa and other parts affected by Bangaru OR Ahirwati. No unique target origin or borrowing edge.
Grierson lists un as an oblique plural demonstrative also used in the singular; the specimen uses it in a personal-reference context.
The source explicitly identifies this first sentence as good Ahirwati.
The source explicitly identifies this second sentence as good Bangaru.
Grierson attributes these past-copula forms to the country around Bawal in Nabha and Kot Kasam in Jaipur; gender pairing of the parenthetical forms is not separately stated.
Grierson describes past-participle bōlō as a Rohtak form with y dropped from bōlyō; he also identifies bōlā as a Bangaru form in this mixed specimen.
Grierson identifies bōlā as a Bangaru form occurring alongside Ahirwati forms in this mixed specimen.

Source explicitly attributes the forms to Hissar and other parts affected by Bangaru AND Ahirwati. Number/gender assignments are not separately printed for this inline group; no automatic pairing to preceding table cells.
Grierson labels this form oblique plural and says it is also often used with singular meaning.
The printed final component thō matches a copula in Grierson’s p. 51 paradigm; this comparison does not classify the entire compound.
The printed final component sū̃ matches a copula in Grierson’s p. 51 paradigm; this comparison does not classify the entire compound.

Source: Bikaner often prefers initial b; Wilson observed the same peculiarity in Sirsa. In other Bagri areas under Panjabi, Bangaru or Ahirwati influence w/v is retained. One printed pair, not repeated printing for every area.
